claim: Imaging is used to map activity across populations of neurons.
source: Imaging is used to map activity across populations of neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement about the application of imaging in neuroscience, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Microscopes with cellular resolution have small (<1 millimeter) fields of view.
source: Microscopes with cellular resolution have small (<1 millimeter) fields of view and cannot simultaneously image activity distributed across multiple brain areas.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the trade-off between resolution and field of view in conventional microscopy.

claim: Microscopes with cellular resolution cannot simultaneously image activity distributed across multiple brain areas.
source: Microscopes with cellular resolution have small (<1 millimeter) fields of view and cannot simultaneously image activity distributed across multiple brain areas.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the small field of view limitation mentioned in the same sentence.

claim: Typical large field of view microscopes do not resolve single cells, especially in the axial dimension.
source: Typical large field of view microscopes do not resolve single cells, especially in the axial dimension.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the limitations of existing large field of view microscopy systems.

claim: The 2p-RAM allows high-resolution imaging anywhere within a volume spanning multiple brain areas (∅ 5 mm x 1 mm cylinder).
source: We developed a 2-photon random access mesoscope (2p-RAM) that allows high-resolution imaging anywhere within a volume spanning multiple brain areas (∅ 5 mm x 1 mm cylinder).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by subsequent experimental data and measurements throughout the paper.

claim: 2p-RAM resolution is near diffraction limited with lateral resolution of 0.66 μm at the center.
source: 2p-RAM resolution is near diffraction limited (lateral, 0.66 μm, axial 4.09 μm at the center; excitation wavelength = 970 nm; numerical aperture = 0.6) over a large range of excitation wavelengths.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of point spread functions using fluorescent beads as shown in Figure 4.

claim: 2p-RAM has axial resolution of 4.09 μm at the center at 970 nm excitation wavelength with NA 0.6.
source: 2p-RAM resolution is near diffraction limited (lateral, 0.66 μm, axial 4.09 μm at the center; excitation wavelength = 970 nm; numerical aperture = 0.6) over a large range of excitation wavelengths.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 2p-RAM has near diffraction-limited resolution over a large range of excitation wavelengths.
source: 2p-RAM resolution is near diffraction limited (lateral, 0.66 μm, axial 4.09 μm at the center; excitation wavelength = 970 nm; numerical aperture = 0.6) over a large range of excitation wavelengths.
evidence: This is supported by measurements at different wavelengths shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: A fast three-dimensional scanning system allows efficient sampling of neural activity in arbitrary regions of interest across the entire imaging volume.
source: A fast three-dimensional scanning system allows efficient sampling of neural activity in arbitrary regions of interest across the entire imaging volume.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the functional imaging experiments shown in Figure 8 and the technical description of the scanning system.

claim: Cellular calcium imaging has become widely used to image activity in neuronal populations over the last ten years.
source: Over the last ten years cellular calcium imaging has become widely used to image activity in neuronal populations (Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles in the field.

claim: Calcium imaging samples activity of all labeled neurons in an imaging volume.
source: Calcium imaging samples activity of all labeled neurons in an imaging volume and can readily be combined with visualization of cell type markers to analyze activity in specific cell types, the nodes of neural circuits (Kerlin et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2014; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work demonstrating this capability.

claim: Calcium imaging can be combined with visualization of cell type markers to analyze activity in specific cell types.
source: Calcium imaging samples activity of all labeled neurons in an imaging volume and can readily be combined with visualization of cell type markers to analyze activity in specific cell types, the nodes of neural circuits (Kerlin et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2014; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The development of sensitive protein sensors for neuronal function has been a major driver for cellular activity imaging in vivo.
source: The development of sensitive protein sensors for neuronal function has been a major driver for cellular activity imaging in vivo (Nagai et al., 2004; Tian et al., 2009; Horikawa et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; Dana et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to key papers describing the development of calcium indicators.

claim: More sensitive indicators allow measurement from larger numbers of neurons at fixed signal-to-noise ratios.
source: More sensitive indicators allow measurement from larger numbers of neurons at fixed signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) (Wilt et al., 2013; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Future improvements in protein sensors are expected to further increase the numbers of neurons that can be probed simultaneously.
source: Future improvements in protein sensors are expected to further increase the numbers of neurons that can be probed simultaneously.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future developments based on current trends.

claim: The vast majority of cellular imaging in vivo has been done with 2-photon microscopy.
source: The vast majority of cellular imaging in vivo has been done with 2-photon microscopy (Denk and Svoboda, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: 2-photon microscopy confines excitation in scattering tissue.
source: 2-photon microscopy confines excitation in scattering tissue, which in turn underlies three-dimensional contrast with subcellular resolution (Denk et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to foundational work and represents established knowledge about 2-photon microscopy.

claim: Confined excitation in 2-photon microscopy underlies three-dimensional contrast with subcellular resolution.
source: 2-photon microscopy confines excitation in scattering tissue, which in turn underlies three-dimensional contrast with subcellular resolution (Denk et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: 2-photon microscopy demands that individual resolution elements (on the order of 1 µm3) are sampled sequentially, limiting its speed.
source: 2-photon microscopy demands that individual resolution elements (on the order of 1 µm3) are sampled sequentially, limiting its speed.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the fundamental operating principle of 2-photon microscopy.

claim: Wide-field methods have been used to measure neural activity, spurred by the development of fast solid state cameras.
source: Spurred by the development of fast solid state cameras, wide-field methods such as wide-field microscopy (Ziv et al., 2013), light-field microscopy (Prevedel et al., 2014), and light-sheet microscopy (Holekamp et al., 2008; Ahrens et al., 2013) have been used to measure neural activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work using these methods.

claim: Scattering and out-of-focus fluorescence rapidly degrade signal and contrast when imaging in scattering tissue with wide-field methods compared to 2-photon microscopy.
source: Scattering and out-of-focus fluorescence rapidly degrade signal and contrast when imaging in scattering tissue with wide-field methods compared to 2-photon microscopy (Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In wide-field imaging, signals from multiple neurons are mixed together at any point in the image.
source: As a consequence, at any point in the image, signals from multiple neurons are mixed together.
evidence: This is an inference from the degradation of signal and contrast mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Unmixing signals to extract neural activity of individual neurons in wide-field imaging is a challenging computational problem, which remains unsolved in general.
source: Unmixing these signals to extract neural activity of individual neurons is a challenging computational problem, which remains unsolved in general.
evidence: This represents current knowledge about the state of computational methods for wide-field imaging analysis.

claim: The high resolution and image contrast provided by 2-photon microscopy allows extraction of fluorescence signals corresponding to the activity of individual neurons and subcellular compartments.
source: In contrast, the high resolution and image contrast provided by 2-photon microscopy allows extraction of fluorescence signals corresponding to the activity of individual neurons and subcellular compartments (Stosiek et al., 2003; Sato et al., 2007; Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013; Petreanu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work demonstrating this capability.

claim: 2-photon microscopy is now routinely used to examine behavior-related activity in populations of neurons.
source: Together with calcium imaging, 2-photon microscopy is now routinely used to examine behavior-related activity in populations of neurons (Harvey et al., 2012; Huber et al., 2012; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The majority of studies image only dozens to hundreds of neurons in one brain region at a time.
source: The majority of studies image only dozens to hundreds of neurons in one brain region at a time.
evidence: This represents knowledge about the current state of the field.

claim: The advent of sensitive protein indicators for calcium and transgenic animals expressing these indicators promises much higher throughput.
source: The advent of sensitive protein indicators for calcium (Nagai et al., 2004; Tian et al., 2009; Horikawa et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013) and transgenic animals expressing these indicators (Dana et al., 2014; Madisen, 2015) promises much higher throughput.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a forward-looking statement based on current developments.

claim: 2-photon microscopy has been used together with GCaMP6 to measure activity in approximately 1800 pyramidal neurons at 7 Hz using 50 mW of power at the sample.
source: 2-photon microscopy has already been used together with GCaMP6 (Chen et al., 2013) to measure activity in approximately 1800 pyramidal neurons at 7 Hz using 50 mW of power at the sample (Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Optimization of the delivered laser power and 2-photon excitation efficiency will allow tracking of more than 10,000 pyramidal neurons at similar signal-to-noise ratios and sampling frequencies.
source: Optimization of the delivered laser power and 2-photon excitation efficiency will allow tracking of more than 10,000 pyramidal neurons at similar signal-to-noise ratios and sampling frequencies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future capabilities based on optimization.

claim: Even relatively simple animal behaviors involve multiple brain regions, which are often non-contiguous.
source: Even relatively simple animal behaviors involve multiple brain regions, which are often non-contiguous (Hernández et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Simultaneous tracking of activity in multiple brain areas is not possible using standard microscopes, because mechanical movement of microscopes or specimens is slow.
source: Simultaneous tracking of activity in these brain areas is not possible using standard microscopes, because mechanical movement of microscopes or specimens is slow.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the limitations of conventional microscopy.

claim: High-resolution microscopes have fields of view that are smaller than most brain areas.
source: High-resolution microscopes have fields of view (FOV) that are smaller than most brain areas, whereas large FOV microscopes have small numerical apertures and cannot resolve individual neurons.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the trade-offs in microscope design.

claim: Large FOV microscopes have small numerical apertures and cannot resolve individual neurons.
source: High-resolution microscopes have fields of view (FOV) that are smaller than most brain areas, whereas large FOV microscopes have small numerical apertures and cannot resolve individual neurons.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the trade-offs in microscope design.

claim: The 2p-RAM is capable of imaging a FOV of 5 mm with subcellular resolution.
source: To bridge the gap between single cells and brain regions we developed a mesoscale 2-photon microscope capable of imaging a FOV of 5 mm, with subcellular resolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The fluorescence signal collected per unit time is ultimately limited by the average power that can be delivered to the specimen, which in turn is limited by heating.
source: The fluorescence signal collected per unit time is ultimately limited by the average power that can be delivered to the specimen, which in turn is limited by heating.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about fundamental limitations in 2-photon microscopy.

claim: In the mouse brain the maximum allowed power is approximately 200 mW.
source: In the mouse brain the maximum allowed power is approximately Pmax = 200 mW (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Serial scanning with a single laser focus maximizes the number of neurons that can be probed given the relatively slow dynamics of calcium-related fluorescence.
source: Given the relatively slow dynamics of calcium-related fluorescence (Peron et al., 2015), serial scanning with a single laser focus maximizes the number of neurons that can be probed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical analysis and citation about calcium dynamics.

claim: Tsai et al designed a scanning system based on off-the-shelf components, producing a scan field of 10 mm.
source: Tsai et al designed an elegant scanning system based on off-the-shelf components, producing a scan field of 10 mm (Tsai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Stirman et al used a custom objective with a field of view of 3.5 mm.
source: Stirman et al used a custom objective (Stirman et al., 2014) with a field of view of 3.5 mm.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The Tsai et al and Stirman et al systems do not provide subcellular resolution in the axial dimension (14 μm and 12 μm, respectively).
source: Neither system provides subcellular resolution in the axial dimension (14 μm and 12 μm, respectively), implying that signals from multiple neurons and neuropil may be conflated.
evidence: This is based on the reported specifications of these systems.

claim: In the Tsai et al and Stirman et al systems, signals from multiple neurons and neuropil may be conflated due to limited axial resolution.
source: Neither system provides subcellular resolution in the axial dimension (14 μm and 12 μm, respectively), implying that signals from multiple neurons and neuropil may be conflated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited axial resolution relative to neuron size.

claim: The Tsai et al and Stirman et al microscopes use standard galvo mirrors, which are too slow for some types of functional imaging.
source: In current implementations these instruments use standard galvo mirrors, which are too slow for some types of functional imaging.
evidence: This represents knowledge about the limitations of these published systems.

claim: The Tsai et al and Stirman et al microscopes do not implement rapid axial scanning.
source: These microscopes also do not implement rapid axial scanning, which is critical for targeting specific neurons in different parts of the FOV.
evidence: This represents knowledge about the capabilities of these published systems.

claim: The Tsai et al and Stirman et al microscopes are corrected for aberrations at only one excitation wavelength (800 nm and 910 nm respectively).
source: In addition, the microscopes are corrected for aberrations at only one excitation wavelength (800 nm and 910 nm respectively), limiting their use to a subset of fluorescent probes.
evidence: This is based on the reported specifications of these systems.

claim: A large FOV (5 mm) mesolens for confocal microscopy, with numerical aperture 0.47, has been reported.
source: A large FOV (5 mm) mesolens for confocal microscopy, with numerical aperture 0.47, has also been reported (McConnell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: 2p-RAM is optimized for imaging populations of neurons in multiple brain regions during behavior.
source: We have developed a 2-photon random access mesoscope (2p-RAM), optimized for imaging populations of neurons in multiple brain regions during behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the in vivo imaging experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: 2p-RAM provides diffraction-limited resolution in a cylindrical volume (∅ 5 mm x 1 mm).
source: 2p-RAM provides diffraction-limited resolution in a cylindrical volume (∅ 5 mm x 1 mm).
evidence: This is supported by the resolution measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: 2p-RAM is fully corrected for excitation light in the 900–1070 nm range.
source: It is fully corrected for excitation light in the 900–1070 nm range, allowing 2-photon imaging of most widely used fluorescent proteins.
evidence: This is supported by measurements at different wavelengths shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: 2p-RAM allows 2-photon imaging of most widely used fluorescent proteins.
source: It is fully corrected for excitation light in the 900–1070 nm range, allowing 2-photon imaging of most widely used fluorescent proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the wavelength range covered and knowledge of fluorescent protein excitation spectra.

claim: 2p-RAM is based on a fast three-dimensional scanning system that allows random access to hundreds of thousands of neurons for targeted interrogation.
source: 2p-RAM is based on a fast three-dimensional scanning system that allows random access to hundreds of thousands of neurons for targeted interrogation.
evidence: This is supported by the technical description of the scanning system and the demonstration of imaging over 200,000 nuclei shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The diameter of the FOV should be five millimeters to allow sampling of most cortical regions in the mouse brain that are nearly coplanar.
source: First, the diameter of the FOV should be five millimeters. This size allows sampling of most cortical regions in the mouse brain that are nearly coplanar.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1A showing the overlay on the mouse cortex.

claim: It would be possible to image the primary somatosensory cortex, the primary motor cortex and parts of secondary motor cortex nearly simultaneously with a 5 mm FOV.
source: For example, it would be possible to image the primary somatosensory cortex, the primary motor cortex and parts of secondary motor cortex nearly simultaneously (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The mesoscope should have better than cellular resolution, implying axial resolutions substantially smaller than the typical size of a soma (diameter, 10 µm).
source: Second, the mesoscope should have better than cellular resolution, implying axial resolutions substantially smaller than the typical size of a soma (diameter, 10 µm) (Peters and Kaiserman-Abramof, 1970).
evidence: This is based on citation about soma size and represents a design criterion.

claim: A numerical aperture of 0.6 translates to approximately 0.61 µm lateral resolution and 4.25 µm axial resolution for λ = 970 nm.
source: We specified a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.6, which translates to approximately 0.61 µm lateral resolution and 4.25 µm axial resolution (for λ = 970 nm; Figure 1B) (Zipfel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on citation to established optical theory and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The mesoscope should produce diffraction-limited performance and high two-photon excitation efficiency over the range of λ = 900–1070 nm.
source: Third, the mesoscope should produce diffraction-limited performance and high two-photon excitation efficiency over the range of λ = 900–1070 nm.
evidence: This is a design specification that is validated by experimental measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The spectral range of 900–1070 nm corresponds to fluorescent protein sensors based on GFP and various red fluorescence proteins.
source: This spectral range corresponds to fluorescent protein sensors based on GFP and various red fluorescence proteins (Akerboom et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents knowledge about fluorescent protein excitation spectra.

claim: The mesoscope should maximize the collection of fluorescence signal, ideally with a large collection NA.
source: Fourth, the mesoscope should maximize the collection of fluorescence signal, ideally with a large collection NA. We specified a collection NA of 1.0 (specifications list in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a design specification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The specified collection NA is 1.0.
source: Fourth, the mesoscope should maximize the collection of fluorescence signal, ideally with a large collection NA. We specified a collection NA of 1.0 (specifications list in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and validated by measurements in Figure 5.

claim: Faster scanning provides better time resolution for measurements of neural activity.
source: Faster scanning provides better time resolution for measurements of neural activity, reduced photodamage, and tracking larger numbers of neurons.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the benefits of faster scanning in microscopy.

claim: Faster scanning provides reduced photodamage.
source: Faster scanning provides better time resolution for measurements of neural activity, reduced photodamage, and tracking larger numbers of neurons.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the benefits of faster scanning in microscopy.

claim: Faster scanning enables tracking larger numbers of neurons.
source: Faster scanning provides better time resolution for measurements of neural activity, reduced photodamage, and tracking larger numbers of neurons.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the benefits of faster scanning in microscopy.

claim: Rapid scanning methods rely on resonant scanning mirrors or acousto optic deflectors.
source: Rapid scanning methods rely on resonant scanning mirrors (Fan et al., 1999) or acousto optic deflectors (AODs) (Reddy and Saggau, 2005), both of which have scan angles on the order of a few degrees, corresponding to relatively small (several hundred μm) scans in the specimen plane.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about scanning technologies.

claim: Resonant scanning mirrors and AODs have scan angles on the order of a few degrees, corresponding to relatively small (several hundred μm) scans in the specimen plane.
source: Rapid scanning methods rely on resonant scanning mirrors (Fan et al., 1999) or acousto optic deflectors (AODs) (Reddy and Saggau, 2005), both of which have scan angles on the order of a few degrees, corresponding to relatively small (several hundred μm) scans in the specimen plane.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the limitations of these scanning technologies.

claim: A lateral scan unit with multiple scanners in series was designed to access the entire scan field rapidly.
source: To access the entire scan field rapidly we designed a lateral scan unit with multiple scanners in series.
evidence: This is a design feature of the 2p-RAM described in the Implementation section.

claim: A fast resonant scan is moved over the specimen in a flexible manner using a galvanometer scanner.
source: A fast resonant scan is moved over the specimen in a flexible manner using a galvanometer scanner, allowing rapid sampling of activity in widely dispersed brain regions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is described in the Implementation section and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: In most scanning microscopes, focusing is achieved by moving the objective.
source: In most scanning microscopes, focusing is achieved by moving the objective.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about conventional microscope design.

claim: Because of the mechanical inertia of the bulky objective, focusing is more than two orders of magnitude slower than lateral scanning.
source: Because of the mechanical inertia of the bulky objective, focusing is more than two orders of magnitude slower than lateral scanning (Göbel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: The structures of interest to be sampled in different brain regions are typically in focal planes that differ by up to several hundred micrometers.
source: This limit is unacceptable for mesoscale imaging because the structures of interest to be sampled in different brain regions are typically in focal planes that differ by up to several hundred micrometers (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1E and represents knowledge about brain anatomy.

claim: A rapid remote focusing unit was implemented in which a light-weight mirror is moved instead of the objective.
source: We addressed this problem by implementing a rapid remote focusing unit in which a light-weight mirror is moved instead of the objective (Botcherby et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a design feature of the 2p-RAM supported by citation to the remote focusing technique.

claim: Rapid remote focusing allowed relaxation of flatness of field specifications, because rapid focusing can partially correct for curved scan fields online.
source: Rapid remote focusing also allowed us to relax flatness of field specifications, because rapid focusing can partially correct for curved scan fields online.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing field curvature correction.

claim: The 2p-RAM was assembled on a vertically mounted breadboard.
source: The 2p-RAM was assembled on a vertically mounted breadboard (Figure 2A,C,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2.

claim: The refractive optics of the microscope are predicted to introduce 25,000 fs2 group-delay dispersion (GDD) at λ = 1000 nm.
source: The refractive optics of the microscope are predicted to introduce 25,000 fs2 group-delay dispersion (GDD) (at λ = 1000 nm).
evidence: This is based on optical modeling of the system.

claim: GDD will cause the light arriving at the focus to be spread out in time, resulting in reduced efficiency for two-photon excitation.
source: GDD will cause the light arriving at the focus to be spread out in time, resulting in reduced efficiency for two-photon excitation (Denk et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about the effects of GDD.

claim: The Ti:Sapphire laser beam first passed through a prism-based GDD compensation unit to reduce GDD at the sample.
source: To reduce GDD at the sample, the Ti:Sapphire laser beam first passed through a prism-based GDD compensation unit (Akturk et al., 2006) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a design feature shown in Figure 2.

claim: With GDD compensation enabled, a pulse width of 106 fs was measured at the sample using an autocorrelator.
source: With GDD compensation enabled, we measured a pulse width of 106 fs at the sample using an autocorrelator (Carpe; APE) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1), comparable to the pulse width emitted by our laser (Mai Tai HP; Spectra Physics).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The measured pulse width at the sample is comparable to the pulse width emitted by the laser.
source: With GDD compensation enabled, we measured a pulse width of 106 fs at the sample using an autocorrelator (Carpe; APE) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1), comparable to the pulse width emitted by our laser (Mai Tai HP; Spectra Physics).
evidence: This is based on comparison of measured data with laser specifications.

claim: The microscope is motorized to allow flexible access to the specimen with >50 mm travel in x, y.
source: The microscope is motorized to allow flexible access to the specimen: it moves in x, y (>50 mm travel); it rotates around an axis that passes through the specimen plane and is parallel to the long axis of the microscope ( ± 20 degrees travel); it moves up and down along the beam axis for coarse focusing (travel +38 mm−13 mm).
evidence: This describes a design feature of the microscope.

claim: The microscope rotates around an axis that passes through the specimen plane and is parallel to the long axis of the microscope with ± 20 degrees travel.
source: The microscope is motorized to allow flexible access to the specimen: it moves in x, y (>50 mm travel); it rotates around an axis that passes through the specimen plane and is parallel to the long axis of the microscope ( ± 20 degrees travel); it moves up and down along the beam axis for coarse focusing (travel +38 mm−13 mm).
evidence: This describes a design feature of the microscope.

claim: The microscope moves up and down along the beam axis for coarse focusing with travel +38 mm−13 mm.
source: The microscope is motorized to allow flexible access to the specimen: it moves in x, y (>50 mm travel); it rotates around an axis that passes through the specimen plane and is parallel to the long axis of the microscope ( ± 20 degrees travel); it moves up and down along the beam axis for coarse focusing (travel +38 mm−13 mm).
evidence: This describes a design feature of the microscope.

claim: The beam was threaded into the microscope through a multi-stage periscope since the microscope moves with respect to the laser.
source: Since the microscope moves with respect to the laser, the beam was threaded into the microscope through a multi-stage periscope.
evidence: This describes a design feature necessitated by the motorized microscope.

claim: The RF unit consists of a custom RF objective and a small mirror (mass, 170 mg) mounted on a voice coil.
source: The RF unit consists of a custom RF objective, and a small mirror (mass, 170 mg; PF03-03-P01, Thorlabs) mounted on a voice coil (LFA 2010 with a sca814 controller; Equipment Solutions).
evidence: This describes the components of the RF unit.

claim: The coatings of the RF objective were optimized for high transmission in the IR range.
source: The coatings of the RF objective were optimized for high transmission in the IR range.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the RF objective.

claim: The coatings and small number of elements (5) of the RF objective combined to give high transmission through the RF objective (97%).
source: These coatings and the small number of elements (5) combined to give high transmission through the RF objective (97%).
evidence: This is measured data about the RF objective performance.

claim: The entrance aperture of the RF objective is conjugated to the entrance aperture of the imaging objective.
source: The entrance aperture of the RF objective is conjugated to the entrance aperture of the imaging objective.
evidence: This describes the optical design of the system.

claim: The RF mirror is approximately conjugate to the focus in the specimen plane.
source: The RF mirror is approximately conjugate to the focus in the specimen plane.
evidence: This describes the optical design of the RF system.

claim: Axial movement of the RF mirror changes the axial location of the focus in the specimen with a scale factor of 1.23.
source: Axial movement of the RF mirror changes the axial location of the focus in the specimen (scale factor, 1.23; i.e. a 100 µm move of the RF mirror causes a 123 µm move of the focus).
evidence: This is measured data about the RF system performance.

claim: For standard microscope objectives, which obey the sine condition, only parallel rays will converge to a diffraction-limited point in the specimen.
source: For standard microscope objectives, which obey the sine condition, only parallel rays will converge to a diffraction-limited point in the specimen (Born and Wolf, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to optical theory.

claim: Spherical wavefronts in the objective pupil will produce spherical aberration at the focus.
source: Spherical wavefronts in the objective pupil will produce spherical aberration at the focus.
evidence: This represents established knowledge from optical theory.

claim: The RF objective was designed to counteract the spherical aberrations produced by the imaging objective.
source: The RF objective was designed to counteract the spherical aberrations produced by the imaging objective, so that diffraction-limited imaging can be achieved throughout the microscope's imaging volume (Botcherby et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a design feature supported by citation to the remote focusing technique.

claim: The imaging objective has axial chromatic aberration that varies with RF depth, which is compensated by the RF objective.
source: The imaging objective also has axial chromatic aberration that varies with RF depth, which is compensated by the RF objective.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the RF objective.

claim: The RF unit allows rapid axial movement of the focal plane, since the RF mirror can be moved much faster than the objective or the specimen.
source: The RF unit allows rapid axial movement of the focal plane, since the RF mirror can be moved much faster than the objective or the specimen.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the step-and-settle measurements in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A resonant scanner produces a fast line scan at 24 kHz line rate.
source: A resonant scanner produces a fast line scan (24 kHz line rate) (CRS 12 K, Cambridge Technology).
evidence: This describes a component of the scanning system.

claim: The resonant scanner has a limited angular range of 10 degrees optical peak-to-peak, resulting in a scan range of 0.6 mm or less in the specimen plane.
source: Because of the limited angular range of the scanner (10 degrees, optical peak-to-peak) this results in a scan range of 0.6 mm or less in the specimen plane.
evidence: This is based on the specifications of the resonant scanner and optical magnification.

claim: The resonant scan line is moved over the specimen using a pair of galvo scanners.
source: This scan line is moved over the specimen using a pair of galvo scanners.
evidence: This describes the scanning system design.

claim: Maintaining conjugation between all scan mirrors and optic pupils is a critical issue for microscopes using remote focusing.
source: Microscopes using remote focusing have to deal with non-planar wavefronts in their pupil locations. Maintaining conjugation between all scan mirrors and optic pupils is a critical issue for these microscopes.
evidence: This represents knowledge about optical design considerations for remote focusing systems.

claim: Movement of any scan mirror that is not conjugated to a subsequent optic pupil will cause a lateral shift of the wavefront at that pupil.
source: Otherwise, the movement of any scan mirror that is not conjugated to a subsequent optic pupil, such as the entrance pupil of the objective, will cause a lateral shift of the wavefront at that pupil.
evidence: This represents knowledge about optical design principles.

claim: Wavefront non-planarity and lateral shift can cause significant optical aberrations.
source: Wavefront non-planarity and lateral shift can cause significant optical aberrations.
evidence: This represents knowledge about optical aberrations.

claim: The VCGP unit conjugates the x and y scan galvo pair without a large-aperture relay made from refractive optics.
source: The VCGP unit conjugates the x and y scan galvo pair without a large-aperture relay made from refractive optics.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the scanning system.

claim: The VCGP provides a compact and cost-effective solution compared to a custom pupil relay using refractive optics.
source: Alternatively conjugation could have been accomplished using a custom pupil relay using refractive optics. However, due to its large size, this relay would be the most complex and expensive part of the microscope. The VCGP provides a compact and cost-effective solution.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of design alternatives.

claim: The VCGP uses three galvo mirrors to ensure that the pupils of the x and y scanning galvos are coincident.
source: The VCGP uses three galvo mirrors (rather than two) to ensure that the pupils of the x and y scanning galvos are coincident.
evidence: This describes the design of the VCGP.

claim: The 20 mm galvo mirrors can perform a step across their entire range with step-and-settle time of 3.4 ms.
source: The 20 mm mirrors can perform a step across their entire range with step-and-settle time of 3.4 ms.
evidence: This is a specification of the galvo mirror performance.

claim: The imaging objective has NA 0.6 and focal length 21 mm.
source: The exit pupil of the VCGP is imaged by another pupil relay (PR3; magnification, 2.3) onto the entrance pupil (diameter, 25.6 mm) of the imaging objective (NA, 0.6, focal length 21 mm) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes the specifications of the imaging objective.

claim: The front lens of the imaging objective has a tip diameter of 15 mm.
source: The front lens has a tip diameter of 15 mm.
evidence: This is a specification of the imaging objective.

claim: The distance between the edge of the front lens and the top of the specimen is 2.7 mm.
source: The distance between the edge of the front lens and the top of the specimen is 2.7 mm.
evidence: This is a specification of the working distance.

claim: The effective working distance of the objective is larger than 3 mm because remote focusing moves the focal plane into the specimen without movement of the objective or specimen.
source: Because remote focusing moves the focal plane into the specimen without movement of the objective or specimen, the effective working distance of the objective is larger than 3 mm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the remote focusing capability.

claim: In vivo imaging is usually performed through a microscope coverglass.
source: In vivo imaging is usually performed through a microscope coverglass (Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Holtmaat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established practice.

claim: The optical system is corrected to operate in a diffraction-limited manner through a # 4 coverglass (450 µm of BK7 glass).
source: The optical system is corrected to operate in a diffraction-limited manner through a # 4 coverglass (450 µm of BK7 glass; equivalent to a stack of three # 1 coverglasses).
evidence: This is a design specification validated by the resolution measurements in Figure 4.

claim: Power transmission through the entire system is 13%.
source: Power transmission through the entire system is 13% (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is measured data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An optional second dichroic mirror allows for an ancillary optical path for one-photon imaging and photostimulation.
source: An optional second dichroic mirror (DM2) allows for an ancillary optical path for one-photon imaging and photostimulation.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the microscope.

claim: A third dichroic mirror divides the fluorescence path into two signals, each directed into one of two GaAsP photomultiplier tubes.
source: A third dichroic mirror (DM3) divides the fluorescence path into two signals, each directed into one of two GaAsP photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) (Hamamatsu H11706-40).
evidence: This describes the fluorescence detection system.

claim: In a 2-photon microscope, the etendue of fluorescence light collection by the objective lens must be matched or exceeded by the etendue of the light detector for optimal detection.
source: In a 2-photon microscope, the etendue of fluorescence light collection by the objective lens must be matched or exceeded by the etendue of the light detector. This condition is critical for optimal detection of precious signal photons.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about optical design for efficient light collection.

claim: For the 2p-RAM the imaging objective collects emitted light with an NA of 1.0 and a collection FOV of 6 mm.
source: For the 2p-RAM the imaging objective collects emitted light with an NA of 1.0, and a collection FOV of 6 mm (Oheim et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a specification of the collection optics supported by citation.

claim: The diameter of the imaging objective pupil relevant for fluorescence detection is 42 mm.
source: The diameter of the imaging objective pupil relevant for fluorescence detection is 42 mm.
evidence: This is a specification of the collection optics.

claim: The etendue of the collected emission light exceeds the etendue of current state-of-the-art PMTs.
source: The etendue of this collected emission light exceeds the etendue of the current state-of-the-art PMTs which have a photocathode diameter of 5 mm and a usable NA of approximately 0.9 (unpublished measurements).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the objective collection etendue with PMT specifications.

claim: It is impossible for all of the fluorescence light collected by the objective to be directed onto the PMT using conventional imaging schemes.
source: This makes it impossible for all of the fluorescence light collected by the objective to be directed onto the PMT using conventional imaging schemes (Mainen et al., 1999; Tsai et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the etendue mismatch, supported by citations.

claim: Oil was used to directly couple a custom-made condenser lens to the glass enveloping the PMT to overcome the etendue mismatch problem.
source: To overcome this problem we used oil to directly couple a custom-made condenser lens to the glass enveloping the PMT.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the collection optics.

claim: Oil coupling allowed the collection NA of the PMT to reach 1.4.
source: This allowed the collection NA of the PMT to reach 1.4.
evidence: This is a measured specification of the collection system.

claim: All of the fluorescence that is collected by the imaging objective is projected onto the PMT for detection (not counting reflection losses).
source: In this manner all of the fluorescence that is collected by the imaging objective is projected onto the PMT for detection (not counting reflection losses).
evidence: This is a claim about the performance of the collection system based on the design.

claim: The collection path does not image the back pupil of the objective onto the PMT.
source: Our collection path does not image the back pupil of the objective onto the PMT (Denk et al., 1995; Mainen et al., 1999), as that design would require significantly more complex collection optics.
evidence: This describes a design choice with citations to alternative approaches.

claim: The spatial distribution of the signal on the PMT photocathode varies with location of the signal source within the sample.
source: As a result, the spatial distribution of the signal on the PMT photocathode varies with location of the signal source within the sample.
evidence: This is an inference from the collection optics design.

claim: The spot size of the projected light from a point source in the sample on the photocathode varies from 1.5 mm to 2.7 mm, depending on the location of the source point.
source: The spot size of the projected light from a point source in the sample on the photocathode varies from 1.5 mm to 2.7 mm, depending on the location of the source point.
evidence: This is measured or calculated data about the collection system.

claim: The microscope image is sensitive to inhomogeneities in the photosensitivity of the PMT photocathode.
source: The microscope image is therefore sensitive to inhomogeneities in the photosensitivity of the PMT photocathode.
evidence: This is an inference from the varying spot size on the photocathode.

claim: For the most critical applications it may be necessary to select PMTs with homogeneous photocathodes or employ computational methods to correct for the inhomogeneity.
source: For the most critical applications it may be necessary to select PMTs with homogeneous photocathodes or employ computational methods to correct for the inhomogeneity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential solutions to the photocathode inhomogeneity issue.

claim: The excitation path was modeled in silico using Zemax.
source: The excitation path, including the RF objective, pupil relays 1–3, and imaging objective, was modeled in silico (Zemax).
evidence: This describes the optical design methodology.

claim: Configurations of optical elements were searched for with diffraction-limited performance and high two-photon excitation efficiency across the ∅ 5x1 mm imaging volume, for excitation wavelengths over the range 900–1070 nm.
source: We searched for configurations of optical elements with diffraction-limited performance and high two-photon excitation efficiency across the ∅ 5x1 mm imaging volume, for excitation wavelengths over the range 900–1070 nm.
evidence: This describes the design optimization criteria.

claim: Performance was assessed using the Strehl ratio (SR), which is a measure of the quality of optical image formation.
source: Performance was assessed using the Strehl ratio (SR), which is a measure of the quality of optical image formation.
evidence: This describes the metric used for optical design evaluation.

claim: Without aberrations an optical system has SR = 1; aberrations drive SR toward zero.
source: Without aberrations an optical system has SR = 1; aberrations drive SR toward zero.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the Strehl ratio.

claim: The design was optimized for SR > 0.8 across the imaging volume, a commonly used criterion for diffraction-limited performance.
source: We optimized for SR > 0.8 across the imaging volume, a commonly used criterion for diffraction-limited performance.
evidence: This describes the design criterion used.

claim: Two-photon excitation efficiency depends on the propagation time delay difference (PTD) for different rays across the pupil of the system.
source: Two-photon excitation efficiency depends on the propagation time delay difference (PTD) for different rays across the pupil of the system (Estrada-Silva et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: For PTD not much less than the pulse duration, the efficiency of two-photon excitation would be severely reduced.
source: For PTD not much less than the pulse duration, the efficiency of two-photon excitation would be severely reduced.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about two-photon excitation.

claim: PTD was kept to less than 50 fs (rms) in the design.
source: PTD was kept to less than 50 fs (rms).
evidence: This is a design specification.

claim: No other microscopy system has been designed with optimization of the PTD as a design criterion.
source: As far as we know no other microscopy system has been designed with optimization of the PTD as a design criterion.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the design approach.

claim: Field curvature was limited to less than 160 µm over the 5 mm FOV.
source: Field curvature was limited to less than 160 µm over the 5 mm FOV.
evidence: This is a design specification validated by measurements in Figure 6.

claim: No stock lenses were used for the custom optical modules.
source: No stock lenses were used for these modules, as doing so in most cases would not allow sufficient control over the tolerances to meet performance specifications.
evidence: This describes a design decision.

claim: The RF objective has 5 elements.
source: The element count for each module was: RF objective, 5; pupil relay 1/2 (identical), 4; pupil relay 3, 6; imaging objective, 6.
evidence: This is a specification of the optical design.

claim: Pupil relay 1/2 each have 4 elements.
source: The element count for each module was: RF objective, 5; pupil relay 1/2 (identical), 4; pupil relay 3, 6; imaging objective, 6.
evidence: This is a specification of the optical design.

claim: Pupil relay 3 has 6 elements.
source: The element count for each module was: RF objective, 5; pupil relay 1/2 (identical), 4; pupil relay 3, 6; imaging objective, 6.
evidence: This is a specification of the optical design.

claim: The imaging objective has 6 elements.
source: The element count for each module was: RF objective, 5; pupil relay 1/2 (identical), 4; pupil relay 3, 6; imaging objective, 6.
evidence: This is a specification of the optical design.

claim: An image of a 1 mm thick bath of fluorescein was acquired at an imaging depth of 500 um to measure signal brightness across the FOV.
source: We acquired an image of a 1 mm thick bath of fluorescein (λ = 970 nm). At an imaging depth of 500 um, brightness was constant up to approximately 2.5 millimeters from the center, beyond which image brightness collapsed (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes an experimental measurement shown in Figure 3.

claim: Brightness was constant up to approximately 2.5 millimeters from the center of the FOV, beyond which image brightness collapsed.
source: At an imaging depth of 500 um, brightness was constant up to approximately 2.5 millimeters from the center, beyond which image brightness collapsed (Figure 3).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The image showed inhomogeneities across the resonant scan (608 µm), apparent as shading in the vertical stripes.
source: The image showed inhomogeneities across the resonant scan (608 µm), apparent as shading in the vertical stripes in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The shading is produced by wave front error introduced by pupil relay 2 during rapid resonant scanning.
source: The shading is produced by wave front error introduced by pupil relay 2 during rapid resonant scanning.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed shading.

claim: Inhomogeneities in brightness within the specified FOV were on the order of 30%.
source: Inhomogeneities in brightness within the specified FOV were on the order of 30% (Figure 3C), including a small dip in brightness in the center of the field (this dip is caused by spatial inhomogeneity in the PMT sensitivity across its photocathode; see below).
evidence: This is measured data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is a small dip in brightness in the center of the field caused by spatial inhomogeneity in the PMT sensitivity across its photocathode.
source: Inhomogeneities in brightness within the specified FOV were on the order of 30% (Figure 3C), including a small dip in brightness in the center of the field (this dip is caused by spatial inhomogeneity in the PMT sensitivity across its photocathode; see below).
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed brightness dip.

claim: Fluorescent microbeads (0.5 μm) were embedded in agar at a dilution of 1:10,000 to measure resolution.
source: Fluorescent microbeads (0.5 μm; Fluoresbrite Calibration Grade YG microspheres CAT# 18859, Polysciences Inc.) were embedded in agar (1.5%; Agarose, Type III-A Sigma A9793) at a dilution of 1:10,000.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation for resolution measurements.

claim: The lateral FWHM of the bead image was 0.66 ± 0.003 μm (SEM).
source: The lateral FWHM of the bead image was 0.66 ± 0.003 μm (SEM) and the axial FWHM was 4.09 ± 0.06 μm (SEM).
evidence: This is measured data from the bead imaging experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The axial FWHM of the bead image was 4.09 ± 0.06 μm (SEM).
source: The lateral FWHM of the bead image was 0.66 ± 0.003 μm (SEM) and the axial FWHM was 4.09 ± 0.06 μm (SEM).
evidence: This is measured data from the bead imaging experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Approximately 2 millimeters from the center of the FOV, the resolution started to degrade gradually.
source: Approximately 2 millimeters from the center of the FOV, the resolution started to degrade gradually (Figure 4I,J,K).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the edge of the FOV (2.5 mm from the center) the lateral FWHM was 0.89 ± 0.006 μm (SEM).
source: At the edge of the FOV (2.5 mm from the center) the lateral FWHM was 0.89 ± 0.006 μm (SEM), and the axial FWHM 6.88 ± 0.07 μm (SEM).
evidence: This is measured data from the bead imaging experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the edge of the FOV (2.5 mm from the center) the axial FWHM was 6.88 ± 0.07 μm (SEM).
source: At the edge of the FOV (2.5 mm from the center) the lateral FWHM was 0.89 ± 0.006 μm (SEM), and the axial FWHM 6.88 ± 0.07 μm (SEM).
evidence: This is measured data from the bead imaging experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the center of the FOV, performance was diffraction-limited up to 1 mm deep into the sample.
source: At the center of the FOV, performance was diffraction-limited up to 1 mm deep into the sample (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Performance was similar at different positions in the field and different imaging depths up to 1 mm into the sample.
source: This performance was similar at different positions in the field and different imaging depths up to 1 mm into the sample (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Resolution was consistent across wavelengths from 900 nm to 1040 nm.
source: Resolution was consistent across wavelengths from 900 nm to 1040 nm (the limit of the tuning range of our Ti:Sapphire laser) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Resolution remained essentially unchanged for small (up to ± 2.5°) tilts of the coverglass with respect to the beam axis.
source: Resolution also remained essentially unchanged for small (up to ± 2.5°) tilts of the coverglass with respect to the beam axis (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The 2p-RAM is capable of subcellular resolution over the entire imaging volume (∅ 5x1 mm cylinder).
source: We conclude that the 2p-RAM is capable of subcellular resolution over the entire imaging volume (∅ 5x1 mm cylinder) and is robust to moderate misalignments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the resolution measurements shown in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: The 2p-RAM is robust to moderate misalignments.
source: We conclude that the 2p-RAM is capable of subcellular resolution over the entire imaging volume (∅ 5x1 mm cylinder) and is robust to moderate misalignments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the coverglass tilt measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The brightness of the imaged beads dropped off towards the edge of the FOV (up to a factor of four 2.5 mm from the center of the FOV).
source: The brightness of the imaged beads dropped off towards the edge of the FOV (up to a factor of four 2.5 mm from the center of the FOV; Figure 4K).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The drop in bead brightness at the edge of the FOV is consistent with the observed increase in the size of the PSF.
source: This is consistent with the observed increase in the size of the PSF (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of brightness and PSF size data.

claim: In 2-photon microscopy, the brightness of objects that are on the order of, or smaller than the diffraction limit are highly sensitive to degradation in the PSF.
source: In 2-photon microscopy, the brightness of objects that are on the order of, or smaller than the diffraction limit are highly sensitive to degradation in the PSF.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about 2-photon microscopy.

claim: Decreased fluorescence collection efficiency at the edges of the FOV could also contribute to dimmer images at the edge of the FOV.
source: Decreased fluorescence collection efficiency at the edges of the FOV could also contribute to dimmer images at the edge of the FOV.
evidence: This is speculation about an additional factor contributing to brightness variation.

claim: Resolution was consistent across the center of the field, suggesting that the dip in brightness at the center of the field is likely due to a dip in PMT sensitivity in the center of the FOV.
source: Conversely, resolution was consistent across the center of the field, (Figure 4I,J) suggesting that the dip in brightness (Figure 3) at the center of the field is likely due to a dip in PMT sensitivity in the center of the FOV (see below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that resolution is consistent but brightness varies.

claim: Biological 2-photon microscopy is typically limited by photodamage produced by excitation light.
source: Biological 2-photon microscopy is typically limited by photodamage produced by excitation light.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about limitations in 2-photon microscopy.

claim: Better detection of fluorescence signal allows reduced excitation for fixed SNR.
source: Better detection of fluorescence signal allows reduced excitation for fixed SNR.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the relationship between detection efficiency and excitation requirements.

claim: Optimizing fluorescence detection is a critical aspect of designing a 2-photon microscope for in vivo imaging.
source: Optimizing fluorescence detection is therefore a critical aspect of designing a 2-photon microscope for in vivo imaging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the photodamage limitation and the benefit of better detection.

claim: In scattering samples the objective numerical aperture and its FOV contribute to fluorescence detection.
source: In scattering samples the objective numerical aperture and its FOV contribute to fluorescence detection (Oheim et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: The PMT signal was remarkably constant across the FOV and beyond.
source: The PMT signal was remarkably constant across the FOV and beyond (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The PMT signal showed a modest dip in the center of the FOV (approximately 20% reduced sensitivity).
source: The signal showed a modest dip in the center of the FOV (approximately 20% reduced sensitivity).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The dip in PMT signal at the center was tracked down to inhomogeneous sensitivity on the PMT photocathode.
source: This dip was tracked down to inhomogeneous sensitivity on the PMT photocathode (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from additional measurements.

claim: The total light entering the objective was roughly proportional to the second power of the NA of the light source.
source: The total light entering the objective was roughly proportional to the second power of the NA (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The signal detected by the PMT was proportional to the signal entering the objective up to NA 1.0.
source: The signal detected by the PMT was proportional to the signal entering the objective up to NA 1.0, the specified NA for fluorescence detection of the imaging objective (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The fluorescence collection system performs nearly optimally across the specified FOV (∅ 5 mm).
source: We conclude that our fluorescence collection system performs nearly optimally across the specified FOV (∅ 5 mm).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collection efficiency measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: The overall transmission of the collection path, including reflection and transmission losses, was 71%.
source: The overall transmission of the collection path, including reflection and transmission losses, was 71%.
evidence: This is measured data about the collection system performance.

claim: A thin and flat fluorescent sample was imaged to characterize the field curvature of the microscope.
source: To characterize the field curvature of the microscope we imaged a thin and flat fluorescent sample (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method shown in Figure 6.

claim: The focal position changed by up to 158 µm at 2.5 mm from the center of the FOV due to field curvature.
source: In this way we mapped the field curvature of the microscope. The focal position changed by up to 158 µm at 2.5 mm from the center of the FOV.
evidence: This is measured data from the field curvature characterization shown in Figure 6.

claim: A field curvature correction was implemented by the RF unit in the scan control software.
source: We implemented a field curvature correction by the RF unit in our scan control software.
evidence: This describes a feature of the microscope control system.

claim: Following a 300 µm step, the RF mirror settles to better than 2.5 µm in 6.77 ± 0.02 ms (SEM).
source: Following a 300 µm step, the RF mirror settles to better than 2.5 µm in 6.77 ± 0.02 ms (SEM) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The field curvature correction was done on a line-by-line basis, using the average position of the resonant mirror during the line as the position to correct.
source: The correction was done on a line-by-line basis, using the average position of the resonant mirror during the line as the position to correct.
evidence: This describes the implementation of the field curvature correction.

claim: This scheme corrects the field curvature associated with movements of the slower galvo mirrors.
source: This scheme corrects the field curvature associated with movements of the slower galvo mirrors (i.e. along the vertical image stripes).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6D showing the correction along vertical stripes.

claim: Field curvature along the resonant scan could not be corrected because the RF unit does not have the necessary bandwidth.
source: Field curvature along the resonant scan could not be corrected in this manner because the RF unit does not have the necessary bandwidth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the speed limitations of the RF system.

claim: Not correcting the field curvature along the resonant axis causes striping artifacts present in the images.
source: Not correcting the field curvature along the resonant axis (Figure 6C, bottom) causes striping artifacts present in the images (Figure 7).
evidence: This is observed in the images shown in Figure 7.

claim: Low magnification images showed the vascular pattern on the surface of the brain in GP5.17 and GP4.3 mice.
source: Superficial images showed the vascular pattern on the surface of the brain (GP5.17, Figure 7A,B; GP4.3, Figure 7C, Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A,B,C and Video 1.

claim: Higher magnification views revealed single neurons and their dendrites.
source: Higher magnification views revealed single neurons and their dendrites (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Resolution and contrast degrade with imaging depth in vivo, caused by aberration and scattering.
source: Resolution and contrast degrade with imaging depth in vivo, caused by aberration and scattering (Ji et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Images of neurons appeared as ring-like structures up to 600 µm deep in the tissue, reflecting GCaMP exclusion from the nucleus and demonstrating subcellular resolution of the 2p-RAM.
source: However, images of neurons appeared as ring-like structures up to 600 µm deep in the tissue (Video 1), reflecting GCaMP exclusion from the nucleus (Tian et al., 2009) and demonstrating subcellular resolution of the 2p-RAM.
evidence: This is observed in Video 1 and supported by citation about GCaMP properties.

claim: Deeper imaging at approximately 450 μm below the surface of the brain revealed the outlines of the layer 4 barrels of the whisker representation area of the somatosensory cortex, and the lower limb and upper limb somatosensory areas.
source: Deeper imaging, approximately 450 μm below the surface of the brain, revealed the outlines of the layer 4 barrels of the whisker representation area of the somatosensory cortex, and the lower limb and upper limb somatosensory areas (Figure 7E,F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A; GP4.3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E,F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Layer 4 has decreased fluorescence because stellate cells do not express fluorescent proteins in GP4.3 mice.
source: Layer 4 has decreased fluorescence because stellate cells do not express fluorescent proteins in these mice (Dana et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation about the expression pattern in these mice.

claim: A total of 207,359 nuclei were detected in the imaging volume in emx1-Cre x lsl h2b-GFP mice.
source: We detected a total of 207,359 nuclei in the volume (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is data from automated analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of detected nuclei (207,359) is a lower bound on the number of neurons accessible for functional imaging in the 2p-RAM.
source: This is a lower bound on the number of neurons accessible for functional imaging in the 2p-RAM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nuclei count representing a subset of accessible neurons.

claim: Individual spines were resolved in mice expressing YFP in a sparse subset of pyramidal neurons.
source: In mice expressing YFP in a sparse subset of pyramidal neurons (YFP-H) (Feng et al., 2000) we were able to resolve individual spines (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neural activity was imaged in behaving mice running on a treadmill in tactile virtual reality.
source: We next imaged neural activity in behaving mice running on a treadmill in tactile virtual reality (Sofroniew et al., 2014, Sofroniew et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm with citations to the methods.

claim: A 4.4 mm x 4.2 mm FOV was imaged at 1.9 Hz in layer 2/3 in GP4.3 mice.
source: We imaged a 4.4 mm x 4.2 mm FOV at 1.9 Hz in layer 2/3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B, Video 2; GP4.3 mice).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and Video 2.

claim: A simple correlation analysis revealed over 3000 active neurons in the large FOV imaging.
source: A simple correlation analysis revealed over 3000 active neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The 2p-RAM can link activity at the level of brain regions and single neurons.
source: The 2p-RAM can link activity at the level of brain regions and single neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Low magnification movies showed activity across multiple brain regions including somatosensory, parietal, and motor areas in GP5.17 mice.
source: For example, low magnification movies showed activity across multiple brain regions including somatosensory, parietal, and motor areas (Figure 8A; GP5.17 mice).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Four widely separated regions (each 600x600 μm2) were imaged at higher speed (9.6 Hz).
source: We then imaged region 1 and three additional, widely separated regions (each 600x600 μm2) at higher speed (9.6 Hz) (Figure 8C, Video 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C and Video 3.

claim: Individual neurons showed fluorescence transients corresponding to trains of action potentials.
source: Individual neurons showed fluorescence transients corresponding to trains of action potentials (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation about GCaMP6 properties and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Some neurons in different areas showed high correlation with the average activity in region 1, whereas others showed uncorrelated activity.
source: Some neurons in the different areas showed high correlation with this average trace, whereas others showed uncorrelated activity (Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D,F and supported by citation.

claim: The 2p-RAM can be used to relate activity across nearly the entire dorsal cortex with the activity of individual neurons in specific areas during behavior.
source: In this manner, the 2p-RAM can be used to relate activity across nearly the entire dorsal cortex with the activity of individual neurons in specific areas during behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: The 2p-RAM has a numerical aperture of 0.6 and an imaging volume corresponding to a ∅5x1 mm cylinder.
source: We designed a 2-photon random access mesoscope (2p-RAM) that allows rapid microscopic investigation of neural tissue over large imaging volumes. The 2p-RAM has a numerical aperture of 0.6 and an imaging volume corresponding to a ∅5x1 mm cylinder.
evidence: This is a summary of the key specifications validated throughout the manuscript.

claim: The imaging volume of the 2p-RAM is approximately 100-fold larger compared to other microscopes with comparable resolution.
source: The imaging volume is approximately 100-fold larger compared to other microscopes with comparable resolution.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the specifications of the 2p-RAM and other published microscopes.

claim: The 2p-RAM is optimized for high-resolution in vivo imaging.
source: The 2p-RAM is optimized for high-resolution in vivo imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the in vivo imaging experiments shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Even faster and more flexible scanning could potentially be achieved using acousto-optic deflectors instead of resonant scanners.
source: Even faster and more flexible scanning could potentially be achieved using acousto-optic deflectors (Duemani Reddy et al., 2008) instead of resonant scanners.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future improvements.

claim: Rapid axial scanning is critical for mesoscale functional imaging in the intact brain.
source: Rapid axial scanning is critical for mesoscale functional imaging in the intact brain.
evidence: This is justified by the need to image neurons at different depths in different brain regions.

claim: Neurons of interest will generally be at different imaging depths in different brain regions.
